analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits for low earners and long-term recipients, paid for by higher payroll taxes including above the income cap.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the last five weeks of a dying Congress, the bill got a committee referral and nothing else: no hearing, no markup, no vote, and only 5 cosponsors when it expired.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would increase the minimum Social Security benefit so that people who worked at least 30 years would not retire below the federal poverty line, add a growing bonus for people who have received benefits for 16 years or more, extend child benefits to full-time college students under 22 whose disabled or deceased parent earned the benefit, and require that these increases not be counted as income when deciding eligibility for other low-income programs. To pay for it, the bill would raise the Social Security payroll tax gradually from 6.2% to 6.5% on employees and employers alike, and apply the tax to earnings above the current wage cap, which high earners' wages above roughly $128,000 currently escape.
analysis.who_benefits: People who worked decades at low wages but retired with benefits below the poverty line; long-term beneficiaries, especially the very old and people who spent most of their adult lives on disability; and children of disabled or deceased workers attending college, who currently lose benefits at 18 or 19.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage workers, long-term beneficiaries, college students

how_it_helps.text: Sets a new minimum benefit tied to the federal poverty guideline, scaled by years worked, so someone with 30 or more years in the workforce (with caregiving years counted) could not receive less than poverty-level benefits [S3].
Adds a benefit increase for anyone who has been eligible for Social Security for at least 16 years, rising with each additional year and reaching its full size after 20 years [S3].
Extends child's benefits to full-time post-secondary students under age 22 whose benefits are based on a parent's disability or death, instead of cutting them off at 18 or 19 [S3].

Bars any of the bill's benefit increases from being counted as income or resources for Medicaid, SNAP, housing assistance, or other means-tested programs, so a raise in Social Security cannot cost someone their other benefits [S3].

Funds the expansion by raising the Social Security payroll tax in steps to 6.5% each for employees and employers by 2024 (13% total for the self-employed) and by making earnings above the taxable maximum subject to the tax on a phased schedule [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Every worker and employer through a payroll tax that rises from 6.2% to 6.5% per side by 2024; self-employed people, who pay both sides, through a rise from 12.4% to 13%; and high earners, who would pay Social Security tax on wages above the current cap without earning proportionally higher benefits.
analysis.who_pays_short: All workers, employers, and high earners

drawbacks.text: The payroll tax increase lands on ordinary workers and their employers, not just the wealthy: the rate rises in steps to 6.5% each for employees and employers by 2024, and the self-employed rate reaches 13% [S3].

Above the current taxable maximum, the bill adds only a 3% benefit factor for the newly taxed earnings, so high earners pay substantially more in taxes than they get back in benefits — a deliberate design choice that makes the bill more progressive but more regressive-feeling to those workers [S3].

The bill was introduced on November 29, 2018, five weeks before the 115th Congress ended, with no hearing scheduled, making serious consideration in that Congress effectively impossible from the start [S5,S1].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is targeted and substantial: it lifts the poorest retirees above the poverty line, rewards long-term beneficiaries, and protects students' benefits. The cost is broad but moderate — a payroll tax increase of three-tenths of a percentage point per side phased in over five years, plus new taxes on high earnings that are only partially offset by benefits. The main honest criticism is not the design but the timing and support: a five-week window and five cosponsors meant the bill was a statement of priorities, not a serious legislative push, and its solvency math was never tested in a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and then to its Social Security Subcommittee in early December 2018, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Gwen Moore introduced the bill on November 29, 2018, joined by four original cosponsors: Reps. Schakowsky, Payne, Hastings, and Wilson of Florida [S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means the same day, the committee with jurisdiction over Social Security [S5].
On December 4, 2018, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Social Security, where it remained [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed, and the bill expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1,S5].
Its total support never grew beyond the sponsor and five Democratic cosponsors [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners whose wages above the taxable maximum would have become subject to Social Security tax are better off, since the tax never arrived; so are employers, who kept the 6.2% rate. Low-income retirees gained nothing, and the benefit cuts they would have been spared never happened either.

for.name: Rep. Gwen Moore
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and authored its benefit and tax provisions.

for.name: 5 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Schakowsky, Payne, Hastings, Wilson of Florida, plus the sponsor's party affiliation)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none was on the Ways and Means Committee leadership that controlled its fate.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over Social Security
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on November 29, 2018, and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill before the Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. Kevin Brady
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration in the five weeks remaining in the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; every named supporter was a Democrat, and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.note: Earnings above the current taxable maximum would have become subject to Social Security tax on a phased schedule, while earning only a small 3% benefit factor on those dollars. The bill's fate left their payroll tax exposure unchanged.
The employer-side payroll tax would have risen in steps to 6.5% by 2024, raising labor costs, and high-wage payrolls above the cap would have been newly taxed. It died, so no cost was incurred.
They pay both the employee and employer shares, so their rate would have climbed from 12.4% to 13%, and income above the cap would have been taxed as well. The bill never advanced.

Extending child's benefits to full-time students under 22 whose disabled or deceased parent earned the benefit would direct additional income toward students and the institutions they attend. The provision never took effect.
